analysis.one_liner: Caps drug cost-sharing, expands ACA subsidies, waives deductibles for basic care, and bans surprise emergency billing.
analysis.headline: Senator Warren's health insurance consumer bill, backed by 7 Senate Democrats, died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have tightened the rules on health insurance: insurers would have to spend at least 85 cents of every premium dollar on medical care, federal or state regulators could block unreasonable premium increases, and Affordable Care Act subsidies would have been made more generous and available to people above the current income ceiling. It would have capped prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 a month per person, waived deductibles for basic care like doctor visits and mental health services, set standards to keep insurance networks adequate, banned surprise billing for emergency care, and undone the 2018 rule that let association health plans skip consumer protections. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy insurance on the ACA marketplaces and people with employer or individual plans: they would pay lower drug copays, no deductible for primary care, mental health visits, generic drugs, or urgent care, richer premium subsidies, and would stop getting surprise bills when an emergency provider was out-of-network. Families stuck in the 'family glitch' who couldn't qualify for subsidies despite unaffordable family coverage would become eligible.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the medical loss ratio floor from 80% to 85%, forcing insurers to spend a larger share of premiums on patient care rather than administration and profit.

Gives the Department of Health and Human Services, or states with approved programs, authority to prohibit unreasonable premium increases after public review of insurer data, including provider contracts.

Expands ACA premium tax credits: the benchmark shifts to gold plans, the 400%-of-poverty income cap is removed, and required premium contributions drop to 0-1% for the lowest incomes and 8.5% for those above the old cap.
Caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per month per person ($500 per family), adjusted for inflation.
Waives deductibles for primary and specialist visits, outpatient mental health and substance use care, generic drugs, and urgent care in standardized marketplace plans and in group health plans.

Fixes the 'family glitch': whether employer coverage is 'affordable' is measured against the cost of family coverage, not just employee-only coverage, letting family members qualify for marketplace subsidies.

Requires network adequacy standards (provider counts, distance, wait times), out-of-network coverage at in-network cost-sharing when no in-network provider is reasonably available, continuity of care for 180 days after a provider is dropped, coverage when a patient reasonably relied on an inaccurate provider directory, and a ban on balance billing for emergency services including ground and air ambulance.

Extends open enrollment to at least 8 weeks, appropriates $480 million for marketplace outreach in 2020 with 4% annual increases, restores navigator program requirements, bars tobacco-based premium surcharges, subjects short-term limited-duration plans to consumer protections, and voids the 2018 Labor Department rule expanding association health plans.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the federal Treasury would bear the open-ended cost of the richer subsidies, cost-sharing reductions, and outreach funding; health insurers would give up profit margin (higher medical loss ratio) and pricing discretion; hospitals, ambulance companies, and doctors would lose the ability to send surprise balance bills; and employers and insurers offering group plans would absorb the cost of waiving deductibles for basic services.

drawbacks.text: The cost-sharing reduction fund is an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') and the enhanced premium credits extend with no income ceiling, so the bill's cost to taxpayers would have been large and uncapped.

Raising the medical loss ratio floor to 85% and capping drug cost-sharing squeezes insurer margins, which could push smaller insurers out of markets and reduce competition — a trade-off an honest supporter would acknowledge.

In exchanges run by the federal government, insurers could offer only the standardized plan at the bronze, silver, and gold levels, reducing plan choice for consumers who want different benefit designs.
The expanded subsidies and credits flow through private insurers, locking in the industry's role as the channel for public health spending rather than creating a public alternative.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are real and large: cheaper drugs, deductible-free basic care, an end to surprise emergency billing, and subsidies reaching people the current law excludes. The honest costs are significant — an uncapped federal commitment to enhanced subsidies and cost-sharing, possible insurer exits from markets under the tighter profit limits, and reduced plan choice where standardized options are mandatory. On balance, the bill was designed to shift money from insurer margins and the Treasury toward insured households, and its main defect was fiscal openness rather than a broken benefit design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2019 and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill on April 11, 2019, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Gillibrand, Harris, Baldwin, Klobuchar, Booker, and Blumenthal.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was its last action.
No hearing, committee markup, floor vote, or further amendment ever occurred during the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept their premium-setting discretion and lower medical-loss obligations, hospitals and ambulance providers kept surprise billing, and the federal government avoided the cost of enhanced subsidies — while families facing high deductibles, drug copays, and premium increases got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sole sponsor.

for.name: Six Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Gillibrand, Harris, Baldwin, Klobuchar, Booker, Blumenthal)

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no committee action in two years.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: All seven Senate sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican-led Finance Committee and Senate majority never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would cut insurer margins (85% medical loss ratio), let regulators block unreasonable premium hikes, and cap drug cost-sharing — but it also expands federal premium subsidies that flow through private insurers, locking in their role as the permanent channel for publicly supported coverage.

industries.industry: Hospitals, emergency physicians, and ambulance providers
industries.note: A ban on balance billing for emergency services and reimbursement rules based on in-network rates would end the surprise-billing practice that leaves patients with large out-of-network charges.

industries.industry: Short-term and association health plan sellers
industries.note: Short-term plans would be pulled under consumer protections, and the 2018 Labor Department rule expanding skimpy association health plans would be voided, closing the loophole these plans rely on to sell coverage without ACA protections.
Group plans would have to waive deductibles for primary care, mental health, generic drugs, and urgent care — a benefit to employees but a new cost for employer-sponsored coverage.
